::: {.letter-metadata}
**Date:** Novr 21st 1861  
**From:** Otterbourne, Winchester.  
**Manuscript:** MS Westcountry Studies Library, Exeter/ Yonge 1861/13
:::

My dear [Miss Smith](people/person_263.qmd),

You must have begun to wonder if the Indian £10 was coming I am sure I did, but here it is at last, in good time I hope. It seems that [Mrs Elphinstone](people/person_482.qmd) has been very ill, and that has prevented her from sending it sooner. I will write to her to acknowledge it as soon as I have heard from you. I am glad to see your three Ks in the [Churchman](organizations/other_62.qmd).[^1] I augur well of them, and the [Banks of the Thorne](other_books/otherbook_275.qmd) are much liked. You will have some sheets of [Mrs Grant](cmy_books/cmybook_43.qmd) very soon, but I had to abridge her a little there was so much more of her than of the others.

Fancy the amazement of some travellers in the train at hearing [Dr Harris](people/person_629.qmd) of Torquay alluring two ladies thither by saying ‘If you will come to Torr I will give you the worst street there’.[^2] You may fancy they were kindred 

[the letter seems to break off here, although the fourth side of the sheet is blank. Possibly CMY forgot she had not signed the letter and posted it like this]

---

[^1]: In an envelope addressed to Miss Ann Smith/ The Rectory/ Old Charlton/ SE and postmarked Winchester 21 November 1861, and on reverse London SE (date illegible). The envelope also contains a piece of paper with sums on it labelled Charlton Rectory.
[^2]: *The Daughters of the Fair Elms* By the Author of *The Wynnes*, a serial which ran in the *Churchman’s Companion* from November 1861.
[^3]: Presumably he was trying to “allure” them into being district visitors in his parish.
